A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. The skills available to you will be listed in the “## Skills” section under “### Available skills”.

### How to use skills

- Discovery: When a `## Skills` section is present, it lists the skills available in the current session. Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. # Issue 5: Too many unrelated states are owned by one component

The central project hook currently handles many different responsibilities:

```text
Project list
Selected project
Selected session
Active tab
Mobile sidebar visibility
Settings visibility
Loading progress
Attention indicators
Session navigation
Project refreshing
Session creation
WebSocket project updates
```

Most of this lives in `useProjectsState`, which is called by `AppContentInner`.

The important React rule is:

> When state inside a hook changes, the component calling that hook renders.

That means something as small as opening the mobile sidebar can render `AppContentInner`:

```text
setSidebarOpen(true)
    ↓
useProjectsState changes
    ↓
AppContentInner renders
    ↓
React checks MainContent, Sidebar, CommandPalette, and QuickSettings
```

Memoization can prevent some children from doing their full work, but React must still reach those boundaries and compare their props.

The same root render can happen for many unrelated actions:

```text
Settings open
Project list refreshes
Selected session changes
Active tab changes
Loading progress changes
Mobile sidebar opens
```

The root is effectively acting like a large electrical panel: every small switch is wired through the same central circuit.

This would look cleaner, but would have the same render behavior:

```tsx
function AppContentInner() {
  const projects = useProjectState();
  const sidebar = useSidebarState();
  const settings = useSettingsState();
  const navigation = useNavigationState();
}
```

All four hooks are still called by `AppContentInner`. A state update in any one of them still renders `AppContentInner`.

The state must be moved into smaller component boundaries or a store/context with selective subscriptions.

   - `MainContent`
   - `ChatInterface`
   - Settings

   - Active workspace tab
   - Navigation/session creation actions

4. Move settings state into a settings host/provider.

   Opening settings should update the settings area without changing the project or chat shell.

   ```text

   MainContent subscribes to selected project/session
   Header subscribes to active tab
   ```

# Issue 8: Every store update rebuilds every UI message

This is a concrete problem in the current code.

The session store holds messages as `NormalizedMessage` objects. Before rendering them, [useChatSessionState.ts](<C:/Users/OMEN6/Desktop/Projects/Paid/ClaudeCodeUI - Siteboon/claudecodeui/src/components/chat/hooks/useChatSessionState.ts:336>) calls:

```tsx
normalizedToChatMessages(storeMessages)
```

That converter loops over the complete message history and constructs brand-new `ChatMessage` objects.

Suppose there are three messages:

```text
Normalized A
Normalized B
Normalized C — currently streaming
```

The UI receives:

```text
Render 1: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C1
Render 2: UI-A2, UI-B2, UI-C2
Render 3: UI-A3, UI-B3, UI-C3
```

Only C changed, but A and B were recreated too.

For JavaScript objects:

```tsx
UI_A1 !== UI_A2
```

They may contain identical text, but they are different objects in memory.

`MessageComponent` is already memoized. Unfortunately, its `message` prop keeps getting a new object:

```tsx
<MessageComponent message={newMessageObject} />
```

Therefore, React sees a changed prop and renders it again.

## What the result should look like

When only the streaming message changes:

```text
Render 1: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C1
Render 2: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C2
Render 3: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C3
```

A and B keep the same objects. Their memoized components can skip rendering.

The store is already partly prepared for this. During a streaming update, it creates a new messages array but retains the existing historical `NormalizedMessage` objects. Only the streaming object is replaced.

The object identity is lost later, inside `normalizedToChatMessages`, because the converter rebuilds everything.

## Why this becomes expensive

For 500 displayed messages and 100 streaming updates:

```text
Current conversion work:
500 messages × 100 updates = 50,000 conversions
```

It also creates thousands of short-lived objects. Those objects eventually need to be cleaned up by JavaScript’s garbage collector.

After preserving unchanged message identities, the meaningful conversion work should be much closer to:

```text
1 changing message × 100 updates = 100 conversions
```

The containing array will still change. That is normal. What matters is that the unchanged objects inside it remain the same.

## Plan for issue 8 — not implemented

1. Add identity-focused tests around the conversion layer.

   The tests should verify that after updating the final streaming message:

   ```text
   previousResult[0] === nextResult[0]
   previousResult[1] === nextResult[1]
   previousResult[last] !== nextResult[last]
   ```

2. Replace the stateless full-history converter with a session-scoped incremental projector.

3. Cache each converted `ChatMessage` using its source `NormalizedMessage` object.

   When the source object is unchanged, return the previously created UI object.

4. Handle tool messages carefully.

   A tool-use UI message can depend on a separate tool-result message. Its cache must consider both:

   ```text
   Tool-use source unchanged
   + Tool-result source unchanged
   = reuse UI message
   ```

   If the tool result changes, rebuild only the affected tool-use UI message.

5. Support cases where one normalized message produces multiple UI messages, such as task notifications with a separate result.

6. Preserve the current message ordering, deduplication, pagination, stable keys, and optimistic-message reconciliation.

7. Leave the existing 100ms streaming buffer unchanged.

   This optimization is about reducing the work performed for each buffered update, not changing how frequently updates are shown.

8. Check `groupConsecutiveTools` after message identity is fixed.

   Normal message rows should begin skipping renders immediately. Tool-group wrapper objects may need a separate cache if profiling shows they still render excessively.

9. Add render counters to `MessageComponent` temporarily and test a long conversation.

   The expected result is:

   ```text
   Historical messages: no new renders during ordinary text streaming
   Current streaming message: renders as text arrives
   Affected tool group: renders only when its tool data changes
   ```

10. Run pagination, tool-result, task-notification, optimistic-message, and streaming tests before removing the temporary counters.

The session store holds messages as `NormalizedMessage` objects. Before rendering them, [useChatSessionState.ts](<C:/Users/OMEN6/Desktop/Projects/Paid/ClaudeCodeUI - Siteboon/claudecodeui/src/components/chat/hooks/useChatSessionState.ts:336>) calls:

```tsx
normalizedToChatMessages(storeMessages)
```

That converter loops over the complete message history and constructs brand-new `ChatMessage` objects.

Suppose there are three messages:

```text
Normalized A
Normalized B
Normalized C — currently streaming
```

The UI receives:

```text
Render 1: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C1
Render 2: UI-A2, UI-B2, UI-C2
Render 3: UI-A3, UI-B3, UI-C3
```

Only C changed, but A and B were recreated too.

For JavaScript objects:

```tsx
UI_A1 !== UI_A2
```

They may contain identical text, but they are different objects in memory.

`MessageComponent` is already memoized. Unfortunately, its `message` prop keeps getting a new object:

```tsx
<MessageComponent message={newMessageObject} />
```

Therefore, React sees a changed prop and renders it again.

## What the result should look like

When only the streaming message changes:

```text
Render 1: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C1
Render 2: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C2
Render 3: UI-A1, UI-B1, UI-C3
```

A and B keep the same objects. Their memoized components can skip rendering.

The store is already partly prepared for this. During a streaming update, it creates a new messages array but retains the existing historical `NormalizedMessage` objects. Only the streaming object is replaced.

The object identity is lost later, inside `normalizedToChatMessages`, because the converter rebuilds everything.

## Why this becomes expensive

For 500 displayed messages and 100 streaming updates:

```text
Current conversion work:
500 messages × 100 updates = 50,000 conversions
```

It also creates thousands of short-lived objects. Those objects eventually need to be cleaned up by JavaScript’s garbage collector.

After preserving unchanged message identities, the meaningful conversion work should be much closer to:

```text
1 changing message × 100 updates = 100 conversions
```

The containing array will still change. That is normal. What matters is that the unchanged objects inside it remain the same.

## Plan for issue 8 — not implemented

1. Add identity-focused tests around the conversion layer.

   The tests should verify that after updating the final streaming message:

   ```text
   previousResult[0] === nextResult[0]
   previousResult[1] === nextResult[1]
   previousResult[last] !== nextResult[last]
   ```

2. Replace the stateless full-history converter with a session-scoped incremental projector.

3. Cache each converted `ChatMessage` using its source `NormalizedMessage` object.

   When the source object is unchanged, return the previously created UI object.

4. Handle tool messages carefully.

   A tool-use UI message can depend on a separate tool-result message. Its cache must consider both:

   ```text
   Tool-use source unchanged
   + Tool-result source unchanged
   = reuse UI message
   ```

   If the tool result changes, rebuild only the affected tool-use UI message.

5. Support cases where one normalized message produces multiple UI messages, such as task notifications with a separate result.

6. Preserve the current message ordering, deduplication, pagination, stable keys, and optimistic-message reconciliation.

7. Leave the existing 100ms streaming buffer unchanged.

   This optimization is about reducing the work performed for each buffered update, not changing how frequently updates are shown.

8. Check `groupConsecutiveTools` after message identity is fixed.

   Normal message rows should begin skipping renders immediately. Tool-group wrapper objects may need a separate cache if profiling shows they still render excessively.

9. Add render counters to `MessageComponent` temporarily and test a long conversation.

   The expected result is:

   ```text
   Historical messages: no new renders during ordinary text streaming
   Current streaming message: renders as text arrives
   Affected tool group: renders only when its tool data changes
   ```

10. Run pagination, tool-result, task-notification, optimistic-message, and streaming tests before removing the temporary counters.

Before taking a destructive action:

- Make sure the action is clearly within the user's request.
- Resolve the exact targets with read-only checks when necessary.
- Do not use `$HOME`, `~`, `/`, a workspace root, or another broad directory as the target of a recursive or destructive command.
- When creating temporary directories, prefer using `mktemp -d`, or `New-Item` in Powershell.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- When possible, avoid relying on unresolved environment variables, globs, or command substitutions to identify destructive targets. Use explicit, validated paths.
- Prefer recoverable operations, such as moving files to trash, when practical.
- If the target or scope is unclear, stop and ask the user.

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. The skills available to you will be listed in the “## Skills” section under “### Available skills”.

### How to use skills

- Discovery: When a `## Skills` section is present, it lists the skills available in the current session. Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`.   2) When `SKILL.md` references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`.   3) If `SKILL.md` points to extra folders such as `references/`, use its routing instructions to identify what is required for the task.   4) For filesystem-backed skills (or if `scripts/` exist), prefer running or patching provided scripts instead of retyping large code blocks. For orchestrator skills, use `skills.read` and the available tools; do not invent a local path.
  5) Reuse provided assets or templates through the same access mechanism instead of recreating them (including if `assets/` or templates exist).

  - If multiple skills apply, choose the minimal set that covers the request and state the order you'll use them.
  - Announce which skills you're using and why. If you skip an obvious skill, say why.

  - Progressive disclosure applies to selecting relevant resources, not partially reading a selected instruction file. Do not load unrelated references, scripts, or assets.
  - Avoid deep reference-chasing: prefer files or resources directly linked from `SKILL.md` unless blocked.
  - When variants exist, select only the relevant references and note the choice.

- Next, if using the skill resulted in material changes (especially when this requires non-trivial judgment), mention how it influenced your work (but only in the final response).

You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents. All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.

When you provide a response in the final channel, that content is immediately delivered back to your parent agent.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: NEW_TASK | MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
You may also see them addressed as to=/root/..., which indicates your identity is /root/...

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides.
